claims.text: Conventional powder-metallurgy or infiltration-processed W–Cu composites contain copper as a discontinuous or poorly connected phase.
Directional solidification or a comparable rapid-consolidation process can form aligned, continuous, nanoscale or interconnected copper channels within a tungsten matrix.
An interconnected copper network provides a low-scattering pathway for heat transport.
Forming an interconnected copper network reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
A fine, stable tungsten matrix retains structural integrity and defect tolerance under irradiation.
Copper is the high-thermal-conductivity phase in the proposed W–Cu composite.
Increasing the connectivity of the copper phase increases the composite's effective thermal conductivity.
A continuous tungsten matrix protects the composite against mechanical and irradiation-induced degradation.
Minimizing the number of high-resistance interfaces facilitates rapid heat removal.
The engineered copper network can improve heat removal without compromising mechanical or irradiation-resistant properties.
The aligned-network W–Cu composite will have higher effective thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable W–Cu composite with randomly distributed or discontinuous copper.
The aligned-network W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to that of the conventional control.
The aligned-network W–Cu composite will retain irradiation resistance comparable to that of the conventional control.
The proposed benefit is intended to hold under high heat flux, cyclic thermal loading, and neutron or charged-particle irradiation relevant to fusion-reactor joints.
The benefit depends on achieving a sufficiently continuous copper phase.
Excessive copper enrichment may compromise tungsten-matrix integrity, mechanical strength, and irradiation resistance.
Long-term stability of the engineered W–Cu network under service conditions remains uncertain.
